newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia says to reshuffle national reserve board.
newsitem.headline: Croatia says to reshuffle national reserve board.

text.p: Croatian Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa said on Monday the government was about to enforce more order into the national reserves after probes revealed malpractices with strategic commodities such as wheat.
Following reorganisation the state reserve board, Drzavno Ravnateljstvo za Robne Rezerve, would become part of the Ministry of Economy, Matesa told a news conference.

He said the cabinet might also consider a change at the top of the board, although findings showed the "mysterious disappearance" of some goods from the state reserves could have occurred under previous management.
The goverment decides on the use of commodities and their sale or purchase, but the board until now has been a separate entity, answerable to parliament.

Apart from sugar, flour and other commodities to supplement consumption in case of national shortages or other emergencies, the state warehouses also contain goods like clothing, footwear and even vehicles.
These were amassed under the communist regime, which was constantly preparing for every eventuality, including a foreign invasion.

But the exact quantity of reserves kept in each former Yugoslav republic before the 1991 breakup was treated as top secret, preventing their optimum management and trade when they were taken over by Croatia.
This turned an estimated 300 million German marks worth of goods into "barren capital", said Economy Minister Davor Stern.

"We inherited the organisation of the reserve commission from the previous system and even I don't quite know what is in them," he said. This was among the first things which would have to be determined.

If it had not been for an affair involving some 50,000 tonnes of "missing" wheat this spring, the extent of disorder in Croatian storages might not have been discovered until it was much too late, Stern said.

The head of the state commodity reserve board said in July an investigation into the state of affairs at local depots had revealed large-scale discrepancies between actual stocks and commidity reserve figures.
Stern said the government also planned to change the role of the board which now allows companies to borrow goods from reserves at a minimum interest.
